## Purpose

This report builds a trusted R summary of BMI by income group and gender, then
provides the R results to compare with the Python/pandas translation in
`translation.ipynb`. The analysis is descriptive and uses the cached classroom
dataset.

## Task 3: Load and inspect the data 

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

nhanes <- read_csv(
  "examples/nhanes-equity/data/nhanes_equity_v6.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

tibble(
  raw_row_count = nrow(nhanes),
  raw_column_count = ncol(nhanes),
  missing_bmi_count = sum(is.na(nhanes$BMI))
)
```

## Task 4: Descriptive BMI summary by IncomeGroup and Gender

Include adults ages 20 through 80, inclusive, with non-missing BMI,
`IncomeGroup`, and `Gender`. The summary reports the number of observations,
mean BMI, and sample standard deviation of BMI for each income and gender
combination. Mean and standard deviation are rounded to one decimal place.

```{r}
nhanes_filtered <- nhanes |>
  filter(
    !is.na(BMI),
    !is.na(IncomeGroup),
    !is.na(Gender),
    !is.na(Age),
    Age >= 20,
    Age <= 80
  )

bmi_summary_pipeline <- nhanes_filtered |>
  group_by(IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_bmi = round(mean(BMI), 1),
    sd_bmi = round(sd(BMI), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(IncomeGroup, Gender)

bmi_summary_pipeline
```

## Task 5: Reusable R function

The function below applies the same filters and summary steps to a data frame.

Its output is checked against the pipeline before it is used for comparison.


```{r}
summarize_bmi_by_income_gender <- function(data) {
  data |>
    filter(
      !is.na(BMI),
      !is.na(IncomeGroup),
      !is.na(Gender),
      !is.na(Age),
      Age >= 20,
      Age <= 80
    ) |>
    group_by(IncomeGroup, Gender) |>
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      mean_bmi = round(mean(BMI), 1),
      sd_bmi = round(sd(BMI), 1),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    arrange(IncomeGroup, Gender)
}

bmi_summary_function <- summarize_bmi_by_income_gender(nhanes)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(bmi_summary_pipeline, bmi_summary_function)))

bmi_summary_function
```

## R parity values

Use these values to complete `parity-table.csv` after running the Python
translation. The grouping labels are the `IncomeGroup` and `Gender` pairs in
the summary table above.

```{r}
tibble(
  raw_row_count = nrow(nhanes),
  raw_column_count = ncol(nhanes),
  filtered_row_count = nrow(nhanes_filtered),
  number_of_groups = nrow(bmi_summary_function)
)
```

For parity, Python must use the same inclusive age range and remove rows missing
any of `BMI`, `IncomeGroup`, `Gender`, or `Age`. R's `sd()` and pandas'
`Series.std()` both use the sample standard deviation by default. Compare group
labels and the rounded mean and SD values, not just the overall row counts. If
any values differ, record the likely cause in the parity table before changing
either implementation.
